chunks.content: Introduction The prevalence of individuals living globally with congenital heart disease has increased by 18.7% from 1990 to 2017, which is related to improved outcomes and population growth [ ]. Correspondingly, in China, the scale of pediatric cardiac care is substantial. According to the “2023 White Book of Chinese Cardiovascular Surgery and Extracorporeal Circulation,” a total of 43,909 cardiovascular surgeries were performed on patients under the age of 18 in 2023 [ ]. This volume underscores an acute and growing need for standardized training protocols for clinical practitioners. Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) is indispensable in this field, playing a key role in the intraoperative guidance and evaluation of cardiac surgeries, which has been shown to significantly reduce mortality and morbidity [ ]. Consequently, it is imperative for pediatric cardiac anesthesiologists to achieve high competency in TEE techniques and the accurate interpretation of images during the perioperative period [ ]. Traditionally, TEE training occurs within the operating room (OR) through an apprenticeship model. However, the OR is a high-stress environment that inherently introduces risks when novice trainees perform TEE maneuvers—a concern particularly acute in pediatric patients due to their fragile anatomical structures. These risks include mechanical trauma, such as esophageal mucosal injury or life-threatening perforation, and airway complications like subglottic edema or vocal cord trauma, which can result in extubation failure [ ]. Additionally, the lack of proficiency in inexperienced operators poses a significant risk of delayed or inaccurate diagnosis, which can negatively impact perioperative management [ ]. To address these challenges, simulation-based medical education has emerged as a promising alternative. This education allows trainees to acquire cognitive and technical procedural skills in a controlled, risk-free environment, potentially improving patient safety and proving more effective than traditional apprenticeship training [ , ]. While the benefits of simulation are recognized, there is limited evidence directly comparing its translation to real-world clinical performance in the demanding field of pediatric TEE. Therefore, the aim of this study was to compare the efficacy of simulation-based training using a dedicated pediatric TEE simulator versus traditional apprenticeship training on live patients, specifically focusing on the improvement of pediatric TEE skills in a real-world clinical setting. Methods Study setting and ethics The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013 revision). This prospective randomized controlled single-center study was first approved by the Ethics committee of the Institutional Review Board of Guangzhou Women and Children’s Medical Center (GWCMC)([2022]273A2025021300) on Oct30, 2022, however, due to the severe Covid situation and epidemic prevention policies, the project didn’t make any progress. On February 13, 2025, we applied for an extension, and it was approved. The progress then registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ( www.chictr.org.cn ; ChiCTR2500105325; principal investigator: Yingyi Xu) on July 02, 2025, and conducted from July 03, 2025 to August 07, 2025, in GWCMC, Guangzhou, China. Deidentified data from this study are available from the authors upon request. All trial participants were briefed in advance and signed informed consent. Participants and randomization A convenience sample of 44 first- through third-year anesthesia residents were recruited who had no prior formal training or clinical rotation experience in pediatric transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Since it was an exploratory clinical study, we did not perform sample size estimates. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio) to either the Simulation group (Group S, n = 22) or the Traditional group (Group T, n = 22) using a computer-generated randomization sequence (Stata 16.0; Stata Corp, College Station, TX, USA). To minimize bias, outcome assessors and data analysts were blinded to the group allocation and tested-instructors, although trainees and train-instructors could not be blinded due to the nature of the educational intervention. Deidentified data from this study are available upon request. Training protocol The training program consisted of three sequential phases: (1) standardized foundational education, (2) group-specific hands-on training, and (3) final live clinical assessment. Phase 1: standardized foundational education (Both Groups) Before group allocation–specific training, all participants received identical foundational instruction to ensure comparable baseline knowledge. This phase consisted of: (1) A 2-hour synchronized online didactic session, mandatory for all residents, covering: basic cardiac anatomy and ultrasound physics, principles of pediatric TEE probe handling and the 11 standardized basic perioperative TEE views (Supplementary File 1). (2) Guided interactive self-learning using a free web-based TEE simulator developed by the Interactive Perioperative Education Group at Toronto General Hospital ( http://pie.med.utoronto.ca/TEE/ ) [ ]. This platform provides standard TEE images, a manipulable 3D heart model, and structured textual guidance for identifying anatomical landmarks and clinical applications. There are also text prompts below each view how to identify the above structures and use this view for diagnosis. There have been previous studies that have successfully used this tool and have also effectively evaluated TEE teaching methods [ ]. This platform provides standard TEE images, a manipulable 3D heart model, and structured textual guidance for identifying anatomical landmarks and clinical applications. There are also text prompts below each view how to identify the above structures and use this view for diagnosis. There have been previous studies that have successfully used this tool and have also effectively evaluated TEE teaching methods [ ]. Attendance was monitored, and all participants completed at least 2 h of standardized foundational training. Additional voluntary self-study outside these sessions was not tracked and was not considered in the analysis. Phase 2: group-specific hands-on training After completion of the foundational phase, residents were randomized into one of two training pathways. Simulation group (Group S) Residents in Group S received one-on-one simulation-based training using a mannequin-based pediatric TEE simulator (BabyWorks ® , CAE Healthcare). The simulator simultaneously displayed: real-time ultrasound images, probe position and imaging plane orientation and a corresponding three-dimensional cardiac model. This multimodal feedback allowed trainees to directly visualize the relationship between probe manipulation and image acquisition. Training was conducted in a structured sequence: observation of the instructor performing a standardized pediatric TEE examination on the simulator and hands-on practice by the trainee on the simulator under direct supervision, focusing on probe manipulation and acquisition of the 11 basic views. Each training session lasted 1 h per trainee. Traditional group (Group T) Residents in Group T received one-on-one apprenticeship-based training in the operating room during routine pediatric cardiac surgery. Training followed a parallel structure: observation of the instructor performing TEE on a live patient, and hands-on TEE performance by the trainee on patients under direct supervision. Each training session also lasted 1 h per trainee. Phase 3: final live clinical assessment One week after completion of the training phase, all residents from both groups underwent a standardized clinical assessment. Trainees were required to obtain the 11 basic TEE views on live pediatric patients (aged 10–18 months). A maximum time limit of 15 min was imposed. During assessment, instructors provided passive supervision only, intervening solely if probe manipulation posed a safety risk. To ensure objectivity, performance was independently evaluated by two TEE board–certified instructors who had not participated in the prior training sessions and assessments included image quality, anatomical visualization, and acquisition efficiency according to predefined criteria. Performance was evaluated using a structured scoring system adapted from Ferrero et al. Each view was scored on a scale of 0 to 10 based on three dimensions: imaging angle (0–2 points), overall clarity (0–2 points), and visualization of specific anatomical structures (0–6 points), yielding a maximum total score of 110 points (Supplementary File 2) [ ]. All live clinical training and assessment procedures were conducted under the passive supervision of the instructor. The supervisor immediately intervened if any of the following occurred: (1) unsafe probe handling or potential risk to the patient, (2) difficulty advancing or positioning the probe, or (3) urgent clinical or surgical requirements. Given the educational nature of the intervention, no formal adverse event schedule was prespecified. Patient-related procedural complications were monitored according to institutional routine. Data collection After basic Pediatric TEE education, each participant took a multiple-choice test. After completing each stage of the training course, all participants completed a practical exam, which was conducted in the operating room or on the pediatric TEE simulator. The participants received final testing on patients in need of surgery one week after the course. These patients all needed TEE for their surgeries. Each resident needed to present 11 basic images within 15 min, an assessment tool used by Ferrero et. in their previous investigations was used for the evaluations in this study [ , ]. This assessment tool contains 11 basic TEE views. Each view has a defined criterion that ranges from 0 to 2 points, including: imaging angle, overall clarity, and visualization of the 3 major anatomical structures associated with each view. All scores were marked by 2 experienced TEE instructors (board-certified attending anesthesiologists). Scorers and data analysts were unaware of treatment assignment groups, and trainees and train-instructors could not be blinded due to the nature of the educational intervention. The scoring criteria are shown in Supplementary File 3. Statistical analysis A formal a priori sample size calculation was not performed due to the fixed cohort size in the residency program; a convenience sample of 44 trainees was enrolled. This study utilized statistical methods such as Chi-square tests, t-tests, and correlation analysis to evaluate differences between two groups. Categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test, while continuous variables (e.g., years since graduation and overall scores) were compared using the t-test. Statistical analysis A formal a priori sample size calculation was not performed due to the fixed cohort size in the residency program; a convenience sample of 44 trainees was enrolled. This study utilized statistical methods such as Chi-square tests, t-tests, and correlation analysis to evaluate differences between two groups. Categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test, while continuous variables (e.g., years since graduation and overall scores) were compared using the t-test. Significant differences were noted in operational scores and times, with p -values less than 0.05 indicating superior outcomes for one group. Results Participant characteristics A total of 46 residents were screened from July 03 to August 07, 2025. Two residents were excluded owing to unwillingness to continue the training. A total of 44 residents received training. The participants characteristics were comparable across different rate groups (Table ) with no statistically significant differences. We administered the same test on knowledge of esophageal ultrasound to each participant prior to training, and the total scores were similar and not significantly different between the two groups (Table ). TEE operation after training One week after training, we recorded all participants’ TEE performances on pediatric patients who were 10–18 months old and planned to receive percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty. All patients were involved in this trial under their parents’ agreements. No adverse events or patient-related procedural complications were observed in either group during the study period. Group S (mean 88.60) scored significantly higher than Group T (mean 64.70) ( p < 0.001). Furthermore, the examination duration (time required to complete the 11-view protocol) was significantly shorter in Group S (447.60 ± 136.90 s) than in Group T (584.50 ± 180.00 s, p = 0.007) (Table ; Fig. ). The scores of Angle/clarity/structures were compared between the two groups The median of the total Angle score of the 11 landmarks was 19.30 in the Group S and 17.00 in the Group T, and the p -value was 0.031. In the total clarity score of 11 landmarks, the median score of Group S was 17.30, and that of Group T was 11.90 ( p < 0.001). Similarly, in the structural score, the median total score was 52.5 in the Group S and 37.5 in the Group T ( p < 0.001) (Fig. ). Comparison of the difference in scores of each landmark between the two groups There was no significant difference in scores between the two groups in the first four landmarks which include : (1) ME 4-chamber view, (2) ME 2-chamber view, (3) ME long-axis view and (4) ME ascending aortic long axis, while the difference in score was statistically significant in landmarks 5–11 which include : (1) ME ascending aortic short axis; (2) ME aortic valve short axis; (3) ME right ventricle inflow-outflow; (4) ME bicaval; (5) ME descending aortic short axis; (6) ME descending aortic long axis and (7) TG midpapillary short axis. The score of Group S was significantly higher than that of Group T ( p < 0.05) (Table ). Discussion Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is a critical cardiac imaging modality essential for anesthesia and perioperative management. However, acquiring and maintaining TEE proficiency demands extensive practice and the accumulation of clinical experience [ ]. Consequently, simulation-based training has emerged as a prominent and effective educational tool in TEE instruction. The present study demonstrates that simulation-based training utilizing a 3D mannequin simulator translates directly into superior live TEE performance within the pediatric population. Specifically, novice residents in the simulation group (Group S) achieved higher image quality and demonstrated greater procedural efficiency compared to those in the traditional apprenticeship group (Group T). By providing residents with the opportunity to practice TEE skills in a controlled, risk-free environment, simulation training helps reduce potential risks associated with real-world patient care [ ]. Previous research has shown that significant advantages in improving learning efficiency, accelerating learning and improving comfort with TEE for cardiovascular medicine fellows compared to traditional training methods [ ]. According to guidelines by Hahn et al. [ ], the views included the mid-esophageal (ME) aortic valve short axis and ME bicaval views require complex, simultaneous manual rotation and tip flexion. Furthermore, transgastric (TG) views require mastering gastric advancement and anteflexion, while imaging the descending aorta necessitates a non-intuitive 180-degree probe rotation. In our study, the advantages of simulation were most pronounced in these technically demanding landmarks (Views 5–11), including the ME ascending aortic short axis, ME aortic valve short axis, and particularly the TG mid-papillary short-axis views. We are considered these views more challenging for novices because they require advanced probe manipulations and a higher degree of 3D anatomical spatial orientation compared to the basic mid-esophageal views. In our study, the advantages of simulation were most pronounced in these technically demanding landmarks (Views 5–11), including the ME ascending aortic short axis, ME aortic valve short axis, and particularly the TG mid-papillary short-axis views. We are considered these views more challenging for novices because they require advanced probe manipulations and a higher degree of 3D anatomical spatial orientation compared to the basic mid-esophageal views. Our results align with previous literature in adult populations, a study found that the simulated training group scored significantly higher on both skill tests and knowledge tests than the non-simulated training group [ ]. Regarding the skills mentioned, the study by Bloch et al. specifically evaluated: (1) Imaging quality scores; (2) Quantification skills (including left ventricular function, fractional area change, and grading of valvular insufficiency); and (3) Clinical interpretation skills (identification of hypovolemia, ventricular failure, and tamponade) [ ]. By demonstrating similar superior outcomes in our study, Group S both in terms of higher clinical scores and shorter examination times further validates the essential role of simulation in improving TEE skills. These findings strongly support the integration of simulation training as a mandatory component of pediatric cardiac anesthesia education. Successful TEE performance requires technical proficiency alongside a sophisticated understanding of pediatric anatomy to ensure safe intubation—a critical concern in small children [ – ]. Our curriculum—comprising only two hours of didactic preparation and one hour of hands-on simulation—demonstrates that foundational TEE competency can be effectively initiated during residency. This model provides a streamlined alternative to prolonged specialized fellowship training for achieving initial clinical proficiency. There are several limitations to this study. First, the fixed size of the residency program necessitated a convenience sample ( n = 44), which may limit the statistical power for secondary outcomes. Second, this study assessed short-term skill acquisition rather than long-term retention or competency. Future TEE education may benefit from combining simulation with clinical practice to reinforce both basic and advanced skills [ , ]. Third, the study was limited to anesthesiology residents; future research should explore personalized and adaptive TEE teaching models [ ]. Lastly, although we observed qualitative improvements in trainee engagement, we did not formally measure confidence or satisfaction using validated scales. Conclusion In summary, this trial provides robust evidence that 3D simulation training significantly improves live TEE performance among novice operators compared to conventional training, contributing valuable insights toward optimizing echocardiography education and enhancing perioperative safety in pediatric cardiac care.
